claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Akay et al., 2014

claims.claim: Genetic deletion of muscle spindles leads to poorer outcomes after spinal cord injury.
claims.source: Input from muscle afferents is important for maintaining normal locomotion in adult mice (Akay et al., 2014) and for the reorganization of supraspinal pathways after spinal cord injury (because genetic deletion of muscle spindles leads to poorer outcomes [Takeoka et al., 2014]).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Takeoka et al., 2014

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 is synthesized by muscle spindles in the periphery.
claims.source: Neurotrophin-3 is synthesized by muscle spindles in the periphery (Copray and Brouwer, 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Copray and Brouwer, 1994

claims.claim: Peripherally administered Neurotrophin-3 can remodel spared corticospinal tract connections and promote sensorimotor recovery in adult and elderly rats after stroke.
claims.source: Recent studies from our group show that peripherally administered Neurotrophin-3 can remodel spared corticospinal tract connections and promote sensorimotor recovery in adult and elderly rats after stroke (Duricki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Duricki et al., 2016

claims.claim: Peripheral treatment with recombinant Neurotrophin-3 has been tested in Phase I and II clinical trials and was found to be safe and well-tolerated.
claims.source: Peripheral treatment with recombinant Neurotrophin-3 has already been tested in Phase I and II clinical trials and was found to be safe and well-tolerated (Parkman et al., 2003; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk, 2007; Sahenk et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Parkman et al., 2003; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk, 2007; Sahenk et al., 2005

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 improved sensory and reflex function in patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A disease.
claims.source: Interestingly, Neurotrophin-3 also improved sensory and reflex function in patients with Charcot Marie Tooth 1A disease, a large diameter fiber sensorimotor neuropathy (Sahenk et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sahenk et al., 2005

claims.claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy in rats was sufficient to elicit changes in the connectivity of proprioceptive afferents to motor neurons resulting in signs of spasticity including hyperreflexia of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes.
claims.source: Here, we established a novel rodent model of spasticity which displays many aspects of functional spasticity observed in humans. The model involves bilateral corticospinal tract lesioning in the pyramids, which was sufficient to elicit changes in the connectivity of proprioceptive afferents to motor neurons resulting in signs of spasticity including hyperreflexia of mono- and polysynaptic reflexes.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claims.claim: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 normalized several spinal reflexes after bilateral pyramidotomy.
claims.source: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 normalized several spinal reflexes.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry.
claims.source: Analysis of neurophysiological properties of the spinal circuitry and of molecular markers revealed that Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry and as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental data and inference from results presented in the manuscript

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
claims.source: Analysis of neurophysiological properties of the spinal circuitry and of molecular markers revealed that Neurotrophin-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry and as a regulator of motor neuron excitability.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental data and inference from results presented in the manuscript

claims.claim: Bilateral transection of the pyramids confirmed that corticospinal tract fibers running ventrally through the pyramids had been cut.
claims.source: The lesion completeness was assessed for all rats at the end of the study with eriochrome cyanine staining of the medulla, which confirmed that corticospinal tract fibers running ventrally through the pyramids had been cut (Figure 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Based on histological data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: The left and right pyramids were almost completely absent in bPYX GFP rats versus uninjured naïve rats.
claims.source: (C) The left and right pyramids were almost completely absent in bPYX GFP rats versus uninjured naïve rats (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 107.4, p<0.0001; bPYX GFP versus naïve p<0.001).
claims.evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of histological data shown in Figure 1C

claims.claim: A greater percentage of bPYX GFP rats exhibited flexor spasms than the percentage that exhibited extensor spasms two weeks post-injury.
claims.source: (D) A greater percentage of bPYX GFP rats exhibited flexor spasms than the percentage that exhibited extensor spasms two weeks post-injury.
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral observation data shown in Figure 1D

claims.claim: Rats showed abnormal forelimb movements and signs of spasticity in the open field after bPYX.
claims.source: (E) Rats showed abnormal forelimb movements and signs of spasticity in the open field after bPYX (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 19.8, p<0.001; bPYX GFP baseline versus all post-injury Weeks, paired t-test p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 1E

claims.claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused rats to make many errors on the horizontal ladder with their treated forelimb as a percentage of the total steps taken.
claims.source: (F) Bilateral pyramidotomy caused rats to make many errors on the horizontal ladder with their treated forelimb as a percentage of the total steps taken (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 123.4, p<0.001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1F

claims.claim: bPYX rats had reduced grip strength with their treated forepaw at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 versus uninjured naïves.
claims.source: (G) Unilateral Grip Strength Test. bPYX rats had reduced grip strength with their treated forepaw at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 versus uninjured naïves (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 145.0, p<0.001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve at Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on grip strength testing data shown in Figure 1G

claims.claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused slight mechanical hypersensitivity.
claims.source: (H) Responses to mechanical stimulation of the treated forepaw were assessed using the automated von Frey test. Bilateral pyramidotomy caused slight mechanical hypersensitivity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 5.2, p=0.019; bPYX GFP vs naïve p = 0.003; bPYX GFP versus naïve at Week 4 and 8, p-values<0.05)
claims.evidence: Based on von Frey testing data shown in Figure 1H

claims.claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy led to a persistent deficit in dexterity.
claims.source: (I) Montoya Staircase Pellet Reaching Test. This test assesses fine motor function of the distal forelimb. The sucrose pellets that were eaten on the treated side were counted. Bilateral pyramidotomy led to a persistent deficit in dexterity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 100.3, p<0.0001; bPYX GFP vs naïve p<0.0001; bPYX GFP versus naïve at weeks 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 post-injury p-values<0.0001).
claims.evidence: Based on staircase pellet reaching test data shown in Figure 1I

claims.claim: Less H-wave depression was observed in bPYX GFP rats two weeks post injury compared to uninjured naïve rats.
claims.source: (K) Frequency-dependent depression: The H-wave was depressed at short inter-stimulus intervals in uninjured naïve rats. Less H-wave depression was observed in bPYX GFP rats two weeks post injury (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 9.8, p<0.0001; uninjured versus bPYX GFP at 2 s, 1 s, 0.5 s, 0.2 s and 0.1 s inter-stimulus interval p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on H-reflex electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1K

claims.claim: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused an increase in hyperreflexia relative to uninjured naïve rats at week 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
claims.source: (L) Data for each rat at each week was analysed by measuring the area under each curve which gives an electrophysiological correlate of hyperreflexia. Bilateral pyramidotomy caused an increase in hyperreflexia relative to uninjured naïve rats at week 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 5.9, p<0.001; bPYX GFP versus naïve p = 0.003; bPYX GFP versus naïve at weeks 2, 6 and 10 post-injury, p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on H-reflex area under curve analysis shown in Figure 1L

claims.claim: bPYX GFP rats had an increased polysynaptic reflex response when the median nerve was stimulated and responses were recorded from the ulnar nerve.
claims.source: (Q) The polysynaptic compound action potentials were quantified by measuring the absolute integral (area under the rectified curve) from 3.5 ms to 12 ms. bPYX GFP rats had an increased polysynaptic reflex response (one-way ANOVA F-value = 4.8, p=0.02; bPYX GFP versus naïve, p-value = 0.02).
claims.evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1Q

claims.claim: bPYX GFP rats had increased polysynaptic responses when the radial nerve was stimulated and responses were recorded from the ulnar nerve.
claims.source: (U) The polysynaptic compound action potentials were quantified by measuring the absolute integral (area under the rectified curve) from 3.5 ms to 12 ms. bPYX GFP rats had increased polysynaptic responses versus uninjured naïve rats (one-way ANOVA F-value = 4.2, p=0.03; bPYX GFP versus naïve, p-value = 0.01).
claims.evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1U

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles at 10 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
claims.source: At the end of the study, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles (e.g., in the ipsilateral but not contralateral biceps brachii) (Figure 2B) as well as in the blood (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in the blood at 10 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
claims.source: At the end of the study, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in treated muscles (e.g., in the ipsilateral but not contralateral biceps brachii) (Figure 2B) as well as in the blood (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in ipsilateral cervical C3-C8 DRGs at 4 weeks after AAV1-NT3 injection.
claims.source: ELISA showed that Neurotrophin-3 protein levels were elevated in ipsilateral (but not contralateral) cervical C3-C8 DRGs (Figure 2D), consistent with retrograde transport of hypothetically either AAV1 particles and/or Neurotrophin-3 protein itself.
claims.evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2D

claims.claim: The AAV1 vector carrying the transgene was not retrogradely transported to the DRG.
claims.source: We found that the AAV1 vector carrying the transgene was not retrogradely transported to the DRG (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Based on qRTPCR data shown in Figure 2E showing absence of human NT-3 mRNA in DRGs

claims.claim: Human Neurotrophin-3 mRNA was not detected in the ipsilateral or contralateral cervical DRGs of rats injected with AAV1-NT3 or AAV1-GFP.
claims.source: In other words, we did not detect human Neurotrophin-3 mRNA in the ipsilateral or contralateral cervical DRGs of rats injected with AAV1-NT3 or AAV1-GFP (Figure 2E) although we did detect a strong signal for human Neurotrophin-3 in positive control samples of human brain cDNA.
claims.evidence: Based on qRTPCR data shown in Figure 2E

claims.claim: The viral vector itself was not retrogradely transported to the DRG, but the neurotrophin-3 protein itself was.
claims.source: Together these results show that the viral vector itself was not retrogradely transported to the DRG, but the neurotrophin-3 protein itself was.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from qRTPCR and ELISA data

claims.claim: Intramuscular treatment using AAV1-NT3 did not significantly increase levels of Neurotrophin-3 protein in homogenates of ipsilateral or contralateral spinal cervical hemicords 4 weeks after injection.
claims.source: Intramuscular treatment using AAV1-NT3 in this cohort did not significantly increase levels of Neurotrophin-3 protein in homogenates of ipsilateral or contralateral spinal cervical hemicords (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) or liver (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) 4 weeks after injection.
claims.evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claims.claim: In rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn.
claims.source: Immunolabeling revealed that, in rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn (Figure 2H) and ipsilateral cervical motor neurons (including in their nuclei) (Figure 2J) relative to AAV1-GFP (Figure 2G,I respectively) but not in contralateral dorsal horn or motor neurons.
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2H

claims.claim: In rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in ipsilateral cervical motor neurons.
claims.source: Immunolabeling revealed that, in rats treated with AAV1-NT3, Neurotrophin-3 protein was increased in neurons of the ipsilateral cervical dorsal horn (Figure 2H) and ipsilateral cervical motor neurons (including in their nuclei) (Figure 2J) relative to AAV1-GFP (Figure 2G,I respectively) but not in contralateral dorsal horn or motor neurons.
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2J

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment led to a reduction of forelimb spasticity which was still ongoing at 10 weeks post-injury and treatment.
claims.source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment led to a reduction of forelimb spasticity which was still ongoing at 10 weeks post-injury and treatment (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 3A

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment reduced signs of spasticity.
claims.source: (A) Neurotrophin-3 treatment reduced signs of spasticity (RM two-way ANOVA, group F = 19.8, p<0.001; bPYX NT3 versus bPYX GFP at Week 6, 8 and 10, p-values<0.05).
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral scoring data shown in Figure 3A

claims.claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 treatment gradually improved precision stepping on the horizontal ladder throughout the 10 weeks testing period.
claims.source: Rats with bilateral pyramidotomy treated with AAV-GFP frequently missed rungs, but intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 treatment gradually improved precision stepping on the horizontal ladder throughout the 10 weeks testing period (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Based on horizontal ladder test data shown in Figure 3B

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treated rats partially recovered grip strength with their treated forelimb.
claims.source: Additionally, Neurotrophin-3 treated rats partially recovered grip strength with their treated forelimb (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Based on grip strength test data shown in Figure 3C

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 did not cause or affect mechanical hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Importantly, Neurotrophin-3 did not cause or affect mechanical hypersensitivity, as expected from human clinical trials (Parkman et al., 2003; Sahenk, 2007; Chaudhry et al., 2000; Coulie et al., 2000; Sahenk et al., 2005) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Based on von Frey test data shown in Figure 3D and supported by citations to clinical trials

claims.claim: Intramuscular AAV-NT3 treatment did not improve recovery on the pellet reaching task after bilateral pyramidotomy.
claims.source: Intramuscular AAV-NT3 treatment did not improve recovery on the pellet reaching task after bilateral pyramidotomy (Figure 3E) which is consistent with the fact that corticospinal injury leads to a persistent deficit in dexterity (Weidner et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Based on staircase pellet reaching test data shown in Figure 3E and supported by citation to Weidner et al., 2001

claims.claim: Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 restored the frequency-dependent depression of the H-wave by 6 weeks post-injury.
claims.source: As described above, rats showed less H-wave depression at inter-stimulus intervals of 5 s and less after bilateral pyramidotomy. Intramuscular overexpression of Neurotrophin-3 restored the frequency-dependent depression of the H-wave by 6 weeks post-injury (Figure 3F,G, Table 1), consistent with injection of AAV-NT3 into this hand muscle.
claims.evidence: Based on H-reflex electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G and Table 1

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 normalised the exaggerated polysynaptic responses that were measured in the ulnar nerve after median nerve stimulation.
claims.source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment also modified polysynaptic spinal reflexes involving afferents from treated muscles. Neurotrophin-3 normalised the exaggerated polysynaptic responses that were measured in the ulnar nerve after median nerve stimulation (Figure 3I–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3J

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treated animals had no reduction of the exaggerated polysynaptic responses recorded in the ulnar nerve after radial nerve stimulation.
claims.source: However, Neurotrophin-3 treated animals had no reduction of the exaggerated polysynaptic responses recorded in the ulnar nerve after radial nerve stimulation (Figure 3K–L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the fact that only flexor muscles were injected with AAV-NT3 and that proprioceptive afferent fibers in the radial nerve (supplying extensor muscles) did not receive direct treatment.
claims.evidence: Based on nerve stimulation electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3L and inference about treatment specificity

claims.claim: After bilateral pyramidotomy, more vGluT1 boutons were found in close proximity to cervical motor neurons of the ulnar and radial nerves.
claims.source: We determined whether the number of vGluT1 immunoreactive boutons in close proximity to motor neurons changed after bilateral pyramidotomy (Figure 4A–C). After injury, more vGluT1 boutons were found in close proximity to cervical motor neurons of the ulnar and radial nerves (Figure 4E) which might contribute to the spasticity we report.
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4E

claims.claim: CTb-immunoreactive afferents from the ulnar nerve had more vGluT1 boutons in close proximity to radial motor neurons after bilateral pyramidotomy.
claims.source: CTb-immunoreactive afferents from the ulnar nerve had more vGluT1 boutons in close proximity to radial motor neurons (Figure 4F). This suggests aberrant strengthening of excitatory afferent connectivity upon antagonists which might mediate increased co-contractions.
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4F and inference about functional consequences

claims.claim: After bilateral pyramidotomy, there were fewer vGAT boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 positive boutons.
claims.source: Analysis of z-stack confocal images revealed vGAT immunoreactive boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 immunoreactive boutons in the ventral horn. After bilateral pyramidotomy, there were fewer vGAT boutons in close proximity to vGluT1 positive boutons (Figure 4K) suggesting they received less presynaptic inhibition by GABAergic interneurons.
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4K and inference about presynaptic inhibition

claims.claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons.
claims.source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4E

claims.claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats.
claims.source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4F

claims.claim: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels.
claims.source: Intramuscular Neurotrophin-3 normalized the number of excitatory vGluT1 boutons onto ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 4D–E), reduced CTb+ ulnar excitatory boutons near to radial motor neurons towards the levels seen in uninjured naïve rats (Figure 4F) and increased apparent presynaptic inhibition of vGluT1 boutons to normal levels (Figure 4J–K).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4K

claims.claim: The number of vGAT immunoreactive inhibitory boutons upon motor neurons was not affected by injury or Neurotrophin-3 treatment.
claims.source: The number of vGAT immunoreactive inhibitory boutons upon motor neurons which mediate post-synaptic inhibition was not affected by injury or Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn.
claims.source: Cervical spinal cord sections were immunolabeled for serotonin and we measured the pixel intensity in the dorsal laminae I/II/III and the ventral horn. Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn; the former was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5B

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment normalized the increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn.
claims.source: Cervical spinal cord sections were immunolabeled for serotonin and we measured the pixel intensity in the dorsal laminae I/II/III and the ventral horn. Corticospinal tract injury resulted in an increase of serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn, but not in the dorsal horn; the former was normalized by Neurotrophin-3 treatment (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry quantification shown in Figure 5B

claims.claim: After injury, there was less KCC2 in the membrane of ulnar and radial motor neurons and more accumulations within the somata.
claims.source: After injury, we found less KCC2 in the membrane of ulnar and radial motor neurons and more accumulations within the somata (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5C,D

claims.claim: Neurotrophin-3 treatment translocated KCC2 back to the membrane of both ulnar and radial motor neurons.
claims.source: Neurotrophin-3 treatment translocated KCC2 back to the membrane of both ulnar and radial motor neurons (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5D

claims.claim: Selective and complete lesioning of the corticospinal tract results in spasticity in the rodent model.
claims.source: Our rodent model gives evidence that selective and complete lesioning of the corticospinal tract results in spasticity.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claims.claim: Damage to the pyramidal tracts is sufficient and necessary to cause spastic hemiplegia in humans.
claims.source: Spasticity symptoms have sometimes been ascribed to additional damage to extrapyramidal structures, but a recent extensive review of pathological cases gives evidence that damage to the pyramidal tracts is sufficient and necessary to cause spastic hemiplegia in humans (de Oliveira-Souza, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to de Oliveira-Souza, 2015

claims.claim: Macaque monkeys with bilateral corticospinal tract injuries in the pyramids were still able to walk and climb shortly after the injury.
claims.source: A large cohort of macaque monkeys received bilateral corticospinal tract injuries in the pyramids. While skilled hand function is severely affected by the lesions, the monkeys were still able to walk and climb shortly after the injury.
claims.evidence: Based on reference to Lawrence and Kuypers' classic experiments

claims.claim: Macaque monkeys with bilateral pyramidotomy exhibited clonic movements, narrowed stance during locomotion, and increased flexor activities in their forelimbs.
claims.source: We re-examined their original videos (Lemon et al., 2012) and observed clonic movements (their Supplementary Videos 2, 3 and 8), narrowed stance during locomotion (their Supplementary Video 6) and increased flexor activities in their forelimbs (their Supplementary Video 7) supporting the notion that corticospinal tract injury is sufficient to produce spastic signs and abnormal locomotion in non-human primates as well as humans.
claims.evidence: Based on re-examination of videos from Lemon et al., 2012

claims.claim: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity.
claims.source: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity (Côté et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 1998; Bose et al., 2002; Corleto et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2008) and after sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms (Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claims.claim: After sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms.
claims.source: After thoracic cord transection or contusion, rats show lower limb spasticity (Côté et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 1998; Bose et al., 2002; Corleto et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2008) and after sacral cord transection rodents displayed tail spasms (Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2004; Kapitza et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2010

claims.claim: A midthoracic T-lesion results in hindlimb spasms during swimming.
claims.source: A midthoracic T-lesion, which essentially damages the dorsomedial, dorsolateral and ventromedial parts of the corticospinal tracts, results in hindlimb spasms during swimming (Gonzenbach et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzenbach et al., 2010

claims.claim: Baclofen is one of the more potent anti-spasticity drugs.
claims.source: One of the more potent anti-spasticity drugs is baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist (Stempien and Tsai, 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Stempien and Tsai, 2000

claims.claim: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons.
claims.source: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons (Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010) plus concurrent increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010

claims.claim: Spasticity is associated with an increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons.
claims.source: Spasticity is associated with a decrease of inhibitory synapses and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials in motor neurons (Kapitza et al., 2012; Kakinohana et al., 2012; Boulenguez et al., 2010) plus concurrent increase of excitatory synapses upon and persistent inward currents in motor neurons (Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2001; Hultborn et al., 2013

claims.claim: Knocking out presynaptic GABAergic interneurons results in limb oscillations during directed reaching for sugar pellets.
claims.source: Functionally, knocking out presynaptic GABAergic interneurons results in limb oscillations during directed reaching for sugar pellets (Fink et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Fink et al., 2014

claims.claim: Mice lacking functional muscle spindles show impaired re-organization of spinal circuitry and restricted locomotor recovery after CNS injury.
claims.source: Indeed, mice lacking functional muscle spindles (lacking proprioceptive feedback) show impaired re-organization of spinal circuitry and restricted locomotor recovery after CNS injury (Takeoka et al., 2014; Akay et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Takeoka et al., 2014 and Akay et al., 2014

claims.claim: Corticospinal axons and proprioceptive afferents compete for synaptic space in the spinal cord in development and also in adulthood.
claims.source: Corticospinal axons and proprioceptive afferents compete for synaptic space in the spinal cord in development and also in adulthood (Jiang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016

claims.claim: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers.
claims.source: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers (Brownstone and Bui, 2010); following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on these interneurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Brownstone and Bui, 2010 and inference about consequences of injury

claims.claim: Following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on premotor interneurons.
claims.source: Premotor interneurons receive direct input from the corticospinal tract and cutaneous and proprioceptive afferent fibers (Brownstone and Bui, 2010); following loss of corticospinal input, proprioceptive afferents may invade the empty synaptic space on these interneurons.
claims.evidence: Inference based on known anatomy and competition for synaptic space

claims.claim: Motor neurons, low threshold cutaneous mechanoceptive afferents and proprioceptive afferents express trkC.
claims.source: Motor neurons, low threshold cutaneous mechanoceptive afferents and proprioceptive afferents express trkC (McMahon et al., 1994), which is the main receptor for neurotrophin-3.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to McMahon et al., 1994

claims.claim: Neurotrophins are retrogradely transported in signaling endosomes after they bind to and are internalized with their receptors.
claims.source: Neurotrophins are retrogradely transported in signaling endosomes (after they bind to and are internalized with their receptors) (Helgren et al., 1997; Harrington et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Helgren et al., 1997; Harrington et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2010

claims.claim: Cutaneous afferents may have modulated spinal reflexes after NT-3 treatment.
claims.source: We expect that the majority of changes in spinal cord patterning and excitability was mediated via proprioceptive afferents and motor neurons. results.result: Bilateral pyramidotomy (bPYX) in rats produces a rodent model of forelimb spasticity. Histological analysis confirmed complete transection of the pyramids. Rats developed behavioral signs of spasticity including flexor spasms, abnormal forelimb movements, errors on the horizontal ladder, reduced grip strength, slight mechanical hypersensitivity, and persistent deficits in dexterity.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C41, C75, and C116 collectively demonstrate that bilateral pyramidotomy produces spasticity in rats. Histological confirmation (C34-C35), behavioral observations (C36-C37), and multiple functional tests (C38-C41) with appropriate statistical analyses provide converging evidence for this novel rodent model of forelimb spasticity.

results.result: Bilateral pyramidotomy caused hyperreflexia of mono- and polysynaptic spinal reflexes. The H-reflex showed reduced frequency-dependent depression at 2-10 weeks post-injury. Polysynaptic reflexes were exaggerated when median or radial nerves were stimulated and responses recorded from the ulnar nerve.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 demonstrate electrophysiological evidence of spinal hyperreflexia after bPYX. The H-reflex data (C42-C43) and polysynaptic reflex measurements (C44-C45) are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures ANOVA, one-way ANOVA) with significant p-values, providing robust evidence for altered spinal reflex excitability.

results.result: Intramuscular AAV1-NT3 injection increased NT-3 protein levels in treated muscles, blood, and ipsilateral cervical DRGs. The viral vector itself was not retrogradely transported to DRGs (no human NT-3 mRNA detected), but NT-3 protein was retrogradely transported. NT-3 protein was also increased in ipsilateral dorsal horn and motor neurons, but not detected at increased levels in spinal cord homogenates overall.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 demonstrate successful NT-3 delivery and biodistribution. ELISA data (C46-C48, C52), qRT-PCR data (C49-C50), and immunohistochemistry (C53-C54) provide converging evidence. The distinction between viral vector transport and protein transport (C51) is well-supported by the combination of qRT-PCR (showing no transgene mRNA) and ELISA (showing increased protein).

results.result: NT-3 treatment reduced forelimb spasticity and improved motor function after bilateral pyramidotomy. NT-3 reduced spasticity scores, improved precision stepping on the horizontal ladder, and partially recovered grip strength. NT-3 did not cause mechanical hypersensitivity and did not improve dexterity on the pellet reaching task.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60, C117, and C120 demonstrate functional benefits of NT-3 treatment. Multiple behavioral tests with appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures ANOVA) show significant improvements in spasticity and locomotion (C55-C58). The lack of effect on mechanical sensitivity (C59) and dexterity (C60) is consistent with the injury model and provides important specificity controls.

results.result: NT-3 treatment normalized spinal reflexes involving afferents from treated muscles. NT-3 restored frequency-dependent depression of the H-reflex by 6 weeks and normalized exaggerated polysynaptic responses when median nerve was stimulated. However, NT-3 did not reduce exaggerated polysynaptic responses after radial nerve stimulation, consistent with selective treatment of flexor muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63, C118-C119 demonstrate selective normalization of spinal reflexes. The H-reflex data (C61) and polysynaptic reflex measurements (C62-C63) show that NT-3 effects are specific to circuits involving treated muscles. The lack of effect on radial-to-ulnar reflexes (C63) provides important specificity control, supporting the interpretation that NT-3 acts via treated muscle afferents.

results.result: Bilateral pyramidotomy increased excitatory vGluT1 boutons on motor neurons and reduced presynaptic inhibition. NT-3 treatment normalized the number of vGluT1 boutons on ulnar and radial motor neurons, reduced aberrant ulnar-to-radial connectivity, and restored presynaptic inhibition to normal levels. Post-synaptic inhibitory boutons (vGAT) on motor neurons were unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 demonstrate anatomical mechanisms underlying spasticity and NT-3 effects. Immunohistochemistry with appropriate quantification shows increased excitatory connectivity after injury (C64-C65), reduced presynaptic inhibition (C66), and normalization by NT-3 (C67-C69). The lack of change in post-synaptic inhibition (C70) provides important specificity. Statistical analyses support all quantitative claims.

results.result: Bilateral pyramidotomy altered serotonergic innervation and KCC2 localization in the spinal cord. Injury increased serotonergic fiber density in the ventral horn and caused KCC2 internalization from motor neuron membranes. NT-3 treatment normalized both serotonergic fiber density and KCC2 membrane localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74, C95, and C122 demonstrate additional mechanisms of spasticity and NT-3 action. Immunohistochemistry with quantification shows changes in serotonergic innervation (C71-C72) and KCC2 localization (C73-C74) after injury, and normalization by NT-3 (C72, C74, C95, C122). These findings are supported by appropriate statistical analyses and provide mechanistic insight into motor neuron hyperexcitability.

results.result: NT-3 acts as a regulator of afferent input connectivity to spinal motor circuitry and motor neuron excitability. NT-3 caused re-balancing of excitatory and inhibitory networks in the spinal cord and normalized serotonergic fiber patterns, contributing to normalization of reflexes and functional recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C93-C94, C96, and C121 represent integrative conclusions based on multiple experimental findings. These mechanistic interpretations are well-supported by the anatomical (vGluT1, vGAT, serotonin, KCC2), electrophysiological (H-reflex, polysynaptic reflexes), and behavioral data presented in the manuscript. The claims appropriately synthesize the experimental evidence.

results.result: Damage to pyramidal tracts is sufficient to cause spastic hemiplegia in humans and non-human primates. Re-examination of videos from macaque monkeys with bilateral pyramidotomy revealed clonic movements, narrowed stance, and increased flexor activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide translational context for the rodent model. C76 is supported by citation to a comprehensive review (de Oliveira-Souza, 2015). C77-C78 are based on re-examination of published videos from classic primate studies (Lemon et al., 2012), providing comparative evidence that corticospinal tract injury alone produces spasticity across species.

results.result: Spasticity is a common and clinically significant problem after spinal cord injury and stroke. Current treatments are symptomatic and have limitations. Modeling spasticity in rodents remains challenging.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 establish the clinical context and rationale for the study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These background claims provide justification for developing a new rodent model of spasticity and testing NT-3 as a therapeutic intervention.

results.result: Previous rodent models of spasticity have examined tail spasms, clonus, and hindlimb spasms during swimming after thoracic or sacral spinal cord injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C79-C81 summarize prior work on rodent models of spasticity. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide context for the novelty of the current forelimb spasticity model after bilateral pyramidotomy.

results.result: Proprioceptive afferents play a major role in regulating spinal motor circuitry, especially after CNS injury. Proposed mechanisms of spasticity include altered connectivity and activity of proprioceptive afferents, reduced inhibition, and increased motor neuron excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C16 provide mechanistic background on proprioceptive circuits and spasticity mechanisms. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These background claims establish the scientific rationale for examining proprioceptive connectivity and motor neuron excitability in the current study.

results.result: NT-3 is required for survival and patterning of sensory and motor neurons during development, can reduce motor neuron excitability, and is synthesized by muscle spindles. NT-3 levels increase after exercise and rehabilitative training. Muscle spindle input is important for locomotion and recovery after CNS injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C26 provide background on NT-3 biology and its relationship to proprioceptive function and recovery. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These background claims establish the rationale for testing NT-3 as a therapeutic intervention for spasticity.

results.result: NT-3 has shown therapeutic potential in preclinical and clinical studies. Peripherally administered NT-3 improved sensorimotor recovery after stroke in rats, was safe and well-tolerated in Phase I/II clinical trials, and improved sensory and reflex function in Charcot Marie Tooth 1A patients. An AAV1-NT3 gene therapy has FDA approval for clinical trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C102-C103 establish the translational potential of NT-3 therapy. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to published studies and clinical trials. These claims provide strong rationale for the translational relevance of the current study and support the feasibility of clinical translation.

results.result: Baclofen is a potent anti-spasticity drug. Spasticity is associated with decreased inhibitory synapses and increased excitatory synapses on motor neurons. Knockout of presynaptic GABAergic interneurons causes limb oscillations. Mice lacking muscle spindles show impaired recovery after CNS injury. Corticospinal axons and proprioceptive afferents compete for synaptic space.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 provide mechanistic context from the literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. C89 is labeled as inference/speculation, which is appropriate given the proposed mechanism. These background claims support the interpretation of the experimental findings.

results.result: Motor neurons and proprioceptive afferents express trkC, the main NT-3 receptor. Neurotrophins are retrogradely transported in signaling endosomes. The authors acknowledge that cutaneous afferents may have contributed to NT-3 effects, though they expect proprioceptive afferents and motor neurons mediated the majority of changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 discuss the cellular basis for NT-3 action. C90-C91 are supported by appropriate citations. C92 is appropriately labeled as speculation and acknowledges alternative mechanisms and limitations in determining the precise cellular targets of NT-3. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Rubrospinal tract neurons express trkC receptors and may contribute to recovery. Neurorehabilitative training and reflex training are mutually reinforcing. Existing anti-spasticity treatments often do not improve movement disorders, whereas NT-3 normalized reflexes and improved locomotion and grip strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 discuss additional mechanisms and compare NT-3 to existing treatments. C97-C100 are supported by appropriate citations. C101 is based on experimental data from the study. These claims appropriately contextualize the findings and highlight the advantages of NT-3 over symptomatic treatments.

results.result: The study used 60 female Lister hooded rats with group sizes of 10 or more per treatment. Motor neurons were retrogradely traced 3 days before terminal experiments. The H-reflex was assessed at baseline and every two weeks post-surgery.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105, C107-C108 describe key methodological details. The sample sizes (C104-C105) are appropriate and justified by citation to previous studies. The experimental timeline (C107-C108) is clearly stated. These methodological claims are well-documented and support reproducibility.

results.result: vGluT1 is a marker for excitatory boutons of proprioceptive and cutaneous afferents. Proprioceptive afferents receive presynaptic inhibition from GABAergic interneurons. Complete spinal cord transection upregulates 5HT2C receptors and incomplete injury leaves spared serotonergic fibers, both contributing to spasticity. KCC2 regulates motor neuron excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115 provide methodological and mechanistic context for the anatomical analyses. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims justify the choice of markers used in the immunohistochemistry experiments and support the interpretation of the findings.
